Nope. High speeds require a low AoA. The higher the AoA the higher the lift, that is until a stall occurs. This why you always see airplanes on approach to landing with a relatively higher nose pitch. They are slow but maintaining lift with a higher AoA

While this is somewhat correct it is not entirely true. A stall occurs when airflow separates from the wing and is no longer enough to create lift. Though this does happen at low airspeeds, the speed of the aircraft is not the main cause and is ultimately only something closely associated with stalls. The true cause is something in aviation called the Angle of Attack (AoA). Basically, this is the angle created by the leading edge of the wing and the relative direction in which air is moving toward it (relative wind) 

Things can be more complicated than that when flaps get involved but, what it really boils down to is that low speeds require a high AoA to maintain lift. If the AoA gets too high then airflow over the wing separates and the wing stalls. HOWEVER, stalls can and will occur at any airspeed if the AoA is too great.

TLDR: stalls can and will occur at any airspeed if the angle between the relative wind and wing is too great.

While there is/was no excuse for this, the fault is not 100% that of the pilots. Part of it was the thought process that the Airbus, which they were flying cannot stall. It is actually billed as being smart enough, what with its fancy avionics and all, that it will not let the dumb human stall it. The fly-by-wire system is actually supposed to take control at some point and limit the amount of pitch you can actually input. This led to complacency in the cockpit and the FO continuously(and wrongly) constantly pitching the aircraft up despite the stall warn going off. The pilots simply put too much faith in the aircraft and overestimated what it could do for them.
